Events.RelatedBody: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in Aspire. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected applications and components. Aspire Dashboard's unauthenticated NotFound route can permit telemetry deletion in both standalone and AppHost-hosted deployments. In standalone deployments using browser-token authentication, it can also expose the browser token. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/microsoft/aspire/issues/22148 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** Critical - **Score:** 9.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N` - **Weakness:** CWE-862 ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Any supported OS - **Architectures:** x64, Arm64 ## Affected Packages ### Standalone Aspire Dashboard Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- Aspire Dashboard | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 Both 13.6.3 and 13.6.4 contain the unauthenticated NotFound route. ### Aspire Dashboard SDK packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-musl-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-musl-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Aspire Dashboard releases through 13.6.4 are affected, whether deployed independently or launched by an Aspire AppHost. For an AppHost using Dashboard SDK packages, check the resolved Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk package versions against the affected ranges above. If the AppHost selects a CLI-bundled Dashboard or a custom Dashboard path, check the version of that Dashboard instead. Aspire ships independently of .NET; installing a .NET runtime or SDK update does not replace the Dashboard. ### How do I fix the issue? Update Aspire Dashboard to version 13.6.5 or later. Neither 13.6.3 nor 13.6.4 is a fixed upgrade target. For container deployments, explicitly set the Dashboard image to `mcr.microsoft.com/aspire/dashboard:13.6.5` and recreate or redeploy the container. Replace older version tags and nightly image references, including those in generated Docker Compose or Kubernetes manifests, with this fixed stable image. Updating AppHost package references alone does not replace an image reference in an existing deployment manifest. For an AppHost using Dashboard SDK packages, update any explicit Aspire.Hosting.AppHost version, including a central package version, to 13.6.5 or later. If that reference is supplied implicitly by Aspire.AppHost.Sdk, update the SDK reference to 13.6.5 or later instead. Restore and rebuild the AppHost, verify that its resolved Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk packages are 13.6.5 or later, and restart the AppHost to run the updated Dashboard. If your AppHost selects a CLI-bundled Dashboard or a custom Dashboard path, update the Dashboard in that selected bundle or location to 13.6.5 or later and restart the AppHost. Updating AppHost package references alone does not replace that Dashboard. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue in the Aspire repository at https://github.com/microsoft/aspire. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Microsoft disclaims all warranties, either express or implied, including the warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. In no event shall Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers be liable for any damages whatsoever including direct, indirect, incidental, consequential, loss of business profits or special damages, even if Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-118740](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-118740) ### Acknowledgements - Weeraphat Srisutham ### Revisions V1.0 (November 10, 2026): Advisory published.

## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in ASP.NET Core. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected applications and components. ASP.NET Core Identity scaffolding templates use the request-supplied email instead of the account's stored email for password-reset and confirmation messages. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/Scaffolding/issues/3959 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 (base score) - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-640 ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Any supported OS - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages Updating scaffolding packages/tools does not repair previously generated application code. Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc contains the affected templates. Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design is a parent package that brings in the MVC generator through a minimum-version dependency. For Design, applicability depends on the resolved MVC generator: a project that independently resolves a fixed MVC version does not become vulnerable merely because it retains an older Design reference. ### 8.0 - standalone packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.23 | 8.0.24 [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.23 | 8.0.24 ### 9.0 - standalone packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.12 | 9.0.13 [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design) | >= 9.0.0, <= 9.0.12 | 9.0.13 ### 10.0 - standalone packages Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) | >= 10.0.0, <= 10.0.2 | 10.0.3 [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design) | >= 10.0.0, <= 10.0.2 | 10.0.3 ### Additional known affected scaffolding prereleases These are exact known affected versions, not continuous prerelease intervals. Version 20.3.0 supports .NET 8, 9, 10 and 11. Install it as a .NET tool, not as a project package reference. The MVC and Design project packages use the separate fixed versions listed above; 20.3.0 is not a version of those packages. ### Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold 20.x Package | Affected version | Patched version --- | --- | --- [Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold) | >= 20.0.0-preview.1.26156.3, <= 20.1.0 | 20.3.0 The 20.x tool contains the vulnerable Identity and Blazor templates for .NET 8.0 through 11.0. ### Affected legacy prereleases The following exact versions also contain affected templates: - [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc) and [Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design): `11.0.0-preview.1.26156.3` and `11.0.0-preview.1.26230.3`. - [Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold-aspnet](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold-aspnet): `10.0.0-rc.1.25458.5` and `10.0.0-rc.1.25468.1`. Apply the generated-code repair below to applications created with these versions. For new scaffolding, use the Microsoft.dotnet-scaffold 20.3.0 tool, which supports .NET 8 through 11. Migrating to that tool is not an update to an MVC or Design project package reference and does not repair previously generated code. ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Check both the installed scaffolding package/tool version and the code it generated. Applications generated with an affected template remain affected after the tool is updated unless their handlers are corrected. The `dotnet-aspnet-codegenerator` command loads generators from the application's dependencies. Check the project's Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGeneration.Design and Microsoft.VisualStudio.Web.CodeGenerators.Mvc references against the versions above; updating only the command-line tool does not replace those project dependencies. For applications created with `dotnet new`, check the selected SDK with `dotnet --version` in the working directory. Events.RelatedBody:
### Environment
- .NET SDK 11.0.100, Microsoft.Testing.Platform, xUnit v3
- Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.AffectedTests 18.14.0-preview
- Local development with several git worktrees of the same repository, plus CI

### What happens
In our measurements, 59 of 63 local runs of our largest test project fell back to running every test. Three causes:

1. **The map identity includes a hash of the whole test assembly.** Adding or editing any single test changes that hash, so the map no longer applies and the whole project runs. In day-to-day work almost every change touches a test, so the selection rarely applies.
2. **Test UIDs are not portable across checkouts.** With xUnit v3, a test UID is derived from the absolute path of the test DLL. A map collected in one worktree (or on a CI agent) shares no UIDs with another checkout. Pinning a `.uniqueid` file per test project works around it, but this is not documented as part of the affected-tests workflow.
3. **Refreshing the map is expensive.** `--collect-test-map` runs the whole project with coverage (about 7 min in CI, over 15 min locally), and that is the only way to get a valid map again after cause 1.

### Expected
- Invalidate per test, not per assembly: a new or changed test method should only add or refresh its own entries, while the other tests keep their mapping.
- One run that executes the new/changed tests plus the tests affected by the changed sources, and updates the map incrementally from that run.
- Stable test identity across checkouts out of the box, or documentation of the supported way to get it.

### Why it matters
Without this, the feature mostly helps when only product code changes and no test is touched, which is rare in practice. With per-test invalidation, our largest project would drop from about 6.5 min to about 2 min per run.

### Alternatives you've considered

Issues.Title: [release/3.1] Reset current_no_gc_region_info after leaving no gc region implicitly
Issues.Body:
Backport https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/73602.

## Customer Impact
Customers reported occasional `System.InvalidOperationException` with message `The NoGCRegion mode was already in progress` when calling `GC.TryStartNoGCRegion`. This is preventing them from using this optimization and impacting their cold start latencies.

## Testing
Customers have tried the fix on .NET 6 overnight and reported the exception never appears again. Meanwhile, there is an unpatched machine and observed 72 exceptions of the same type in the same time interval, proving this does fix the bug.

## Risk
Low. This only impact customer using `TryStartNoGCRegion`, and this is the right thing to do.

Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Assembly version for DispatchProxy shim is too low resulting in duplicate types for DispatchProxy
Issues.Body:
Create a new `netstandard2.1` library.
Add a reference to `<PackageReference Include="System.Reflection.DispatchProxy" Version="4.7.1" />`
Try to use `DispatchProxy`

Expected: 
`DispatchProxy` is resolved from `netstandard.dll`

Actual:
```
error CS0433: The type 'DispatchProxy' exists in both 'System.Reflection.DispatchProxy, Version=4.0.6.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a' and 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51'
```


Build contains conflict message:
```
Encountered conflict between 'CopyLocal:C:\src\dotnet\runtime\artifacts\bin\testPackages\cache\system.reflection.dispatchproxy\4.7.1\lib\netstandard2.0\System.Reflection.DispatchProxy.dll' and 'Runtime:C:\Program Files\dotnet\packs\NETStandard.Library.Ref\2.1.0\ref\netstandard2.1\System.Reflection.DispatchProxy.dll'. Choosing 'CopyLocal:C:\src\dotnet\runtime\artifacts\bin\testPackages\cache\system.reflection.dispatchproxy\4.7.1\lib\netstandard2.0\System.Reflection.DispatchProxy.dll' because AssemblyVersion '4.0.6.0' is greater than '4.0.5.0'.
```

Other shims avoid this by setting the AssemblyVersion higher than that which was previously shipped.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Assembly version for DispatchProxy shim is too low resulting in duplicate types for DispatchProxy" (#1791)

Issues.Title: Confusing behavior when using AssemblyInfo.cs
Issues.Body:
I'm completely perplexed.

I created a .Net Standard 2.0 library project.

I explicity added an AssemblyInfo.cs file, we need this because we use this utility to "stamp" our assemblies when we build them:

https://github.com/ygoe/NetRevisionTool

That utility is run as a pre/post build event and temporarily replaces placeholders in the AssemblyInformationalVersion attribute with runtime values (like repo folder name, commit ID, branch etc etc).

The completed assembly then has this info "burned" into it as we go forward.

.Net Standard is not working with this.

1. It seems to populatethe Package Version (in the project's Package section) with whatever we put into AssemblyInfo.cs for AssemblyInformationalVersion.
2. The version of the generated nuget package is always set as 1.0.0.

This is just mind blowing, is there no way we can do this seemingly simple operation any more if adopt .Net Standard?
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Confusing behavior when using AssemblyInfo.cs " (#1775)

Issues.Title: Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions
Issues.Body:
I was looking through this repository to determine if .NET Standard 2.1 libraries support default interface methods - it looks like they do, given the presence of `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces`, as well as my own experimenting in VS 2019. It seems I was mistaken when thinking that this was not the case, so I'm glad this repository is easily accessible to determine this.

But while doing this, I found it difficult to determine what commits were included in this particular .NET Standard version. I see that there's a tag `v2.1.0-prerelease.19126.1`, as well as branches `release/2.0.0`, `release/3.0`, and `release/3.0-preview9`. One of the machines I tested VS 2019 on had a `netstandard.dll` assembly, itself targeting .NETStandard v2.1.0, with AssemblyInformationalVersion `1.1.0+a5b5f2e1e369972c8ff1e2183979fab6099f52ef`; this commit is part of the `release/3.0` branch. However, another machine had a same-named assembly, targeting .NETCoreApp v3.0 and AssemblyInformationalVersion `3.0.0+4ac4c0367003fe3973a3648eb0715ddb0e3bbcea`, and I don't see that commit hash in this repository.

Additionally, [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/) states that 2.1 will be the last version, but there is another prerelease tag `v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1` and [on GitHub](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/releases/tag/v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1) it's labelled .NET 5.0 Preview 2.

So I have a few questions for understanding this repository:

1. Since .NET Standard 2.1 is released, are there plans to continue development in this repository for e.g. the shared BCL going forward with .NET 5+?
2. Are there multiple kinds of `netstandard.dll` for a single .NET Standard version? E.g. are there separate versions for .NET Framework to reference and for .NET Core / .NET 5+ to reference?
3. Do the tags / branch names in this repository correspond to a .NET Standard version or something else?
4. It looks like there are patch releases; are there patch versions of a single .NET Standard version?
5. Are there other repositories which are being used to create `netstandard.dll`?
6. Is there a way to determine, from the repository, which commit is the one used for a given release?

Thank you for your consideration.

Issues.Title: Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1
Issues.Body:
# Summary

.NET Standard version is not resolved correctly when a transitive dependency targets multiple .NET Standard versions.

# Environment

- Windows 10 (19042.746)
- .NET 5 SDK 5.0.201

# Minimal reproducible example
[bug.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/files/6209239/bug.zip)

This is a three-project solution:
- `TestProject1` targeting `netcoreapp3.1`
- `ClassProject1` targeting `netstandard2.0`
- `ClassProject2` targeting *both* `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1`

The project dependency chain is: `TestProject1 -> ClassProject1 -> ClassProject2`

A method (`ClassProject2Test1`) on `ClassProject2` is hidden behind a `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

# The issue

The unit test failed with a `MissingMethodException`

```
[xUnit.net 00:00:00.38]     TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [FAIL]
  Failed TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [2 ms]
  Error Message:
   System.MissingMethodException : Method not found: 'Void ClassLibrary2.Class2.Class2Test1()'.
  Stack Trace:
     at ClassLibrary1.Class1.Class1Test1()
   at TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1() in C:\Users\rex\source\netstandard-bug-repro\TestProject1\UnitTest1.cs:line 12
```

# Expected result

The compiler should have resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.0)*` 

# Actual result

The compiler resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.1)*` 

Which causes the exception because the offending method, `ClassProject2Test1`, was hidden by the `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

Issues.Title: Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions
Issues.Body:
### Problem
There is a security vulnerability with the version of System.Text.RegularExpressions that is used by dotnet standard. The vulnerable version of System.Text.RegularExpressions is 4.3.0. Please see links below for the vulnerability documentation or discussion:

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/vulnerability/CVE-2019-0820
https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/111
https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2019-0820
https://snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-DOTNET-SYSTEMTEXTREGULAREXPRESSIONS-174708
https://www.whitesourcesoftware.com/vulnerability-database/CVE-2019-0820

The dotnet commit that fixed the vulnerability is https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/commit/19d4b1163d8a03dd90ff5fd1785eea6305112545

### Issue:
We use whitesource and it has caught this issue with high severity. We don't consume System.Text.RegularExpressions directly but packages that use this. Therefore as a transitive dependency due to NetStandard library, which is being used by several other dotnet packages like Castle Windsor, MassTransit etc., Once an update is available the others could followup and update.

### Code:

[The latest version 2.0.3 of Net standard ](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) still seem to be using System.Text.RegularExpressions version 4.3.0 as per https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/src/apicompat/netstandard/netstandard.depproj

### Fix
Please update[ library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) targeting .netStandard 1.6 to update System.Text.RegularExpression package to latest secured version 4.3.1 to fix the security issue or kindly suggest alternatives.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions" (#1786)

Issues.Title: linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem
Issues.Body:
Hello,

I am currently using .NET core 2.2.x and EF Core. 2.2.6. I have a function that returns a List<Animal> from the database with no issue. It returns 11 results. However, when I try to use `.Where(p => p.DeletedAt.GetValueOrDefault(DateTime.Now) => DateTime.Now).ToList()`, it still should return 11 results, however it returns 0. I also eliminated the possibility that there is something wrong with my where clause (logic) because it works perfectly on 4.6.1 EF Core 2.2.6. Furthermore, I confirmed that it is only where I am comparing a nullable type using that function and I am guessing that I missed a thread someone opened on this issue. I am aware .NET core 2.2 is not LTS. I also thought this goes here because it's not AFAIK, an EF core issue but rather an Ienumerable/Linq issue.

Update: As it turns out your notion of `DateTime.Now` getting evaluated twice is true. To rectify that, I will now be using `DateTime.Now.Date`. This is odd because this exact code works on 4.6.1. You're probably right. SMH. Thank you @GrabYourPitchforks! You may now close.

Microsoft (R) .NET Framework Strong Name Utility Version 4.0.30319.0

Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll is a delay-signed or test-signed assembly

Additional information:

- This issue looks very similar to [this](https://www.damirscorner.com/blog/posts/20140502-StrongNameValidationFailedSecurityException.html)

Issues.Title: System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings slow
Issues.Body:
_This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity2.visualstudio.com/t/SystemDrawingPrintingPrinterSettings-/890524)._ --- Hello I'm debugging a problem with the printer settings. Some calls are significant slower if the default printer is a network printer, even if I explicit set a local printer name. After studying referencesource I think I found the culprit. I call: var printerSettings = new System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings(); printerSettings.PrinterName = "LOCALPRINTER"; // the next call is slow if the OS default printer is a network printer var res = printerSettings.DefaultPageSettings.PrinterResolution Internally FastDeviceCapabilities is called. FastDeviceCapabilities calls GetOutputPort. But GetOutput port return the port of the default printer and not the port of the given printer! In addition, DeviceCapabilities is then called with a wrong combination of printer name and port, don't know if this could lead to additional problems. Resolution: GetOutputPort should return the port of the given printer and not accessing the default printer at all. Best Regards, Raphael --- ### Original Comments #### Raphael Affolter on 1/20/2020, 04:03 AM:

I forgot to mention: .Net Framework 4.6.1

Issues.Title: Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF
Issues.Body:
I'm working on converting a large WPF solution's projects to SDK style and ran into some issues.

The solution is large with multiple projects(old style) all targeting .net452 and some nugets(some made by me) installed, targeting both .net452 and .netstandard2.1 This all seems to work fine, somehow the nuget manages to install the correct version targeting .net452.

I have decided to slowly convert the projects inside the solution to SDK style targeting .net452 and .netstandard2.1 just like the nugets.

This is where the problem starts, one project was converted so far that is referenced by multiple other projects. Localy everything seems to build and run fine, however when Azure DevOps(VS version 2019) is used to build the solution there are 2 scenarios:

1. The famous error message is shown:

                "Error CS0012: The type 'Object' is defined in an assembly that is not referenced. You must add a reference to assembly 
                 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0"

2. It builds fine but on app launch it crashes with:

                 "Could not load file or assembly 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' 
                 or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified."

I'm suspecting that the problem is related to referencing the SDK project, it looks like that somehow it references the .netstandard2.1 instead of the .net452.

The reason this is my suspicion is that if targetframework is set to only .net452 on the referenced project everything works fine. Google has led me to two possible solutions to tell the project what framework to use from the reference:

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj"
                  AdditionalProperties="TargetFramework=net452">
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
and

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj">
      <SetTargetFramework>TargetFramework=net452</SetTargetFramework>
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <<Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
This doesn't look like it's doing anything and the problem still persists. At the moment I ran out of ideas and I'm here asking for help. Please let me know what I'm doing wrong or what else I can try.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

Issues.Title: Fix RSA OAEP decryption in OpenSSL with non-power-of-two keys lengths
Issues.Body:
## Customer Impact

A customer reported in dotnet/runtime#71607 that decrypting RSA OAEP with SHA2 and a 3072-bit key on Linux resulted in a OAEP de-padding error, while other platforms were able to perform these operations successfully.

Investigation in to the issue led to uncover that RSA OAEP decryption that uses the managed implementation does not work with non-power-of-two keys because we do not slice a rented buffer accordingly. The current implementation only works because `CryptoPool.Rent` happens to give back power-of-two arrays which are exactly the same size as the key.

The fix is to slice the data to the correct size.

This does not affect dotnet/runtime because the managed implementation of RSA OAEP is no longer used for OpenSSL RSA decryption. This change was introduced in dotnet/runtime#50063.

## Testing

Unit tests were introduced to test RSA OAEP encryption with a 3072-bit RSA key. These tests will be forward-ported to dotnet/runtime.

## Risk

Minimal. The change is localized and understood that a `Slice` was missing.

Issues.Title: Add Microsoft Learn links to LSP hover
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Add optional Microsoft Learn links to LSP `textDocument/hover` results for C# and Visual Basic types, members, and language keywords. Links should be emitted only for clients that advertise Markdown hover support; plain-text hover output should remain unchanged.

## Motivation

Roslyn already resolves semantic symbols and determines help terms for Visual Studio F1 help, but non-Visual Studio LSP clients cannot use Visual Studio’s help infrastructure. This prevents VS Code and other LSP clients from exposing equivalent documentation links.

## Proposed behavior

### Types and members

Generate Microsoft Learn API links from `ISymbol.GetDocumentationCommentId()` for types, constructors, methods, properties, fields, events, and operators where a reliable destination can be produced.

Aliases, locals, parameters, arrays, nullable values, and constructed generics should be normalized to the relevant original or underlying documented symbol where appropriate. Unsupported overloaded-member mappings should fall back to the containing type page or omit the link rather than produce a broken URL.

Examples:

```text
T:System.Collections.Generic.List`1
→ https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.list-1

M:System.String.Contains(System.String)
→ https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.string.contains

T:Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.ISymbol
→ https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.isymbol
```

Roslyn APIs from official `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis*` assemblies should use the same mapping. A `view=roslyn-dotnet-*` query can be omitted initially unless the referenced package version can be determined reliably.

Conceptual Roslyn SDK documentation is outside the scope of this proposal.

### Language keywords

Add separate C# and Visual Basic mappings from syntax context to Microsoft Learn language-reference pages. Unambiguous keywords can use curated tables, while contextual keywords should reuse Roslyn syntax classification, including cases such as:

- `partial` on a type versus a method
- `default` in a switch, expression, or constraint
- `new` as an operator, modifier, or constraint
- `ref` in parameter, return, local, and type contexts
- `var`, which does not map directly to a same-named page

## Restricting eligible symbols

Namespace matching is insufficient because third-party assemblies can define types in `System.*` or `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.*`.

A symbol should receive a generated link only when:

1. It is a metadata symbol.
2. Its `IAssemblySymbol` resolves to a compilation metadata reference.
3. The reference has verifiable, allowlisted provenance.

Initial provenance allowlist:

- `Microsoft.NETCore.App.Ref`
- `NETStandard.Library.Ref`
- .NET Framework reference assemblies
- Official `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.*` NuGet references
- The SDK `Roslyn/bincore` directory

Provenance should be derived primarily from `PortableExecutableReference.FilePath`. Assembly identity and public-key tokens may supplement this check but should not be the sole test. Source symbols, project references, arbitrary NuGet packages, unresolved symbols, and references without trustworthy provenance should not receive generated links.

## Hover format

For Markdown-capable clients, append a concise link to existing hover content:

```markdown
[View documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.string)
```

Existing declaration, documentation, diagnostic content, and section ordering should remain intact. Omit links for unsupported targets, unresolved symbols, plain-text clients, or mappings that cannot produce a reliable URL.

## Implementation approach

1. Add an internal documentation-link service independent of the Visual Studio layer.
2. Add providers for BCL/Roslyn API links and C#/VB keywords.
3. Integrate the service into `HoverHandler`.
4. Convert canonical symbol documentation IDs into Microsoft Learn API URLs.
5. Cache assembly-provenance decisions for the lifetime of a compilation.
6. Reuse or extract applicable symbol/help-term logic from Visual Studio F1 help without changing that behavior.

## Delivery stages

1. **MVP:** BCL types and straightforward members.
2. Add official Roslyn types and members.
3. Add unambiguous C# and Visual Basic keywords.
4. Add contextual keywords and complex member overloads.
5. Consider version-specific Roslyn API views.

## Acceptance criteria

- Hovering an allowlisted BCL or Roslyn type/member produces a valid Microsoft Learn API link.
- Hovering a source-defined or untrusted third-party symbol does not produce a generated link.
- Keyword links resolve to the correct contextual language-reference page.
- Plain-text hover remains unchanged.
- Existing hover content and ordering remain intact.
- Hover performance is not materially affected.

## Testing

Cover BCL and Roslyn types/members, nested and generic types, overloaded and generic members, constructors, nullable and array types, operators, contextual C#/VB keywords, third-party namespace collisions, source symbols, invalid documentation IDs, missing provenance, and Markdown versus plain-text clients.

## Non-goals

- Mapping arbitrary third-party NuGet APIs
- Generating links for project-defined APIs
- Linking conceptual Roslyn SDK guides
- Replacing Visual Studio F1 help
- Requiring a client-specific LSP extension

Issues.Title: Pick a file name that isn't in use when moving static members to a new type
Issues.Body:
Fixes #61471

Move Static Members to a new type overwrote an existing file when a file with the target name already existed in the folder.

Change (`ExtractTypeHelpers.AddTypeToNewFileAsync`): before creating the document, the code now calls a new `GetUniqueFileName` helper. If no document in the project already uses the name in that directory, the name is used as-is; otherwise the first unused `Name1.cs`, `Name2.cs`, … is picked (number inserted before the extension; collision checked with `GetDocumentIdsWithFilePath`, scoped to the same project). The new type is created in that new file and the existing file is left untouched. This follows the maintainer's direction on the issue: "Just pick a filename that isn't in use."

Test (`CSharpMoveStaticMembersTests.TestMoveFieldNewTypeFileAlreadyExists`, WorkItem 61471): the existing `Class1Helpers.cs` stays byte-identical and the moved member lands in a new `Class1Helpers1.cs`.

Verification: `dotnet build` of the `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.EditorFeatures.UnitTests` project succeeds with 0 warnings and 0 errors. A direct logic check of `GetUniqueFileName` against an `AdhocWorkspace` solution passes 4/4 (no collision → unchanged; one collision → `Class1Helpers1.cs`; two collisions → `Class1Helpers2.cs`; same name in another project → no collision). The xUnit tests were not run locally (the test project targets net472 only, which cannot execute on Linux) — CI should run `TestMoveFieldNewTypeFileAlreadyExists` and the rest of `CSharpMoveStaticMembersTests`.

Issues.Title: Do not report IDE0100 when the comparison performs a user-defined implicit conversion to bool
Issues.Body:
Fixes #86479

The IDE0100 analyzer reported a redundant-equality diagnostic on comparisons like `flag == true` where `flag` is a user-defined type with an implicit conversion to `bool`. Removing the comparison would drop the conversion and change the meaning of the code (or break the build, e.g. `(flag).CompareTo(false)` where `Flag` has no `CompareTo`), so the comparison is not redundant.

Change (`AbstractRemoveRedundantEqualityDiagnosticAnalyzer.AnalyzeOperator`): before reporting, check the non-literal operand — if it is an `IConversionOperation` whose conversion is user-defined and implicit, no diagnostic is reported. The guard sits in the shared abstract analyzer, so it covers both the `==`/`!=` path and the `is true`/`is false` path. An explicit cast in source, `(bool)flag == true`, is still reported: the code fix keeps the cast, so the conversion is preserved. This mirrors the existing skip for overloaded `==`.

Tests (`RemoveRedundantEqualityTests`, WorkItem 86479): `TestUserDefinedImplicitConversionToBool_NoDiagnostics` (`flag == true`, `Flag.Off == false`, `true == flag` produce no diagnostic) and `TestExplicitCastToBool` (`(bool)flag == true` still reports, fix keeps the cast).

Verification: a direct analyzer harness running the real built analyzer against the issue's repro code passes 3/3 (implicit conversion: 0 diagnostics; explicit cast: 1 diagnostic; plain `bool x == true` control: 1 diagnostic). With the guard temporarily reverted, the harness fails the implicit case exactly as reported. `dotnet build` of the CodeStyle unit-tests project succeeds with 0 errors. The xUnit tests were not run locally (the testhost is unusable in this Linux environment) — CI should run `RemoveRedundantEqualityTests`.

Issues.Title: Ensure analyzer config files are location-independent
Issues.Body:
**Problem:** the globalconfig file which the default .net sdk generates for any project contains a full path in `build_property.ProjectDir` option value. Razor's generated globalconfig file also includes full paths in named sections (because each razor file has some options specified for it that the razor source generator then reads) - in general, globalconfig files currently support only full paths.

But this makes any caching system that considers those files' contents (e.g., [BuildXL](https://github.com/microsoft/BuildXL)) unusable across different locations (e.g., git worktrees, or different CI setups).

**Solution proposal:**

1. In roslyn: support relative paths in section names of globalconfig files.
2. In sdk: when generating globalconfig files, use relative paths in section names. (Might be opt-in under some msbuild property, which eg roslyn caching mode would implicitly enable.)
3. In roslyn: add support for "virtual" `build_property.ProjectDir` config property - even if that's not part of any analyzer config, the compiler can provide it.
I'm thinking this could be also opt-in, and configurable, e.g., the SDK would add `virtual_project_dir = ProjectDir, MSBuildProjectDirectory` which would tell the compiler to handle those.
4. In sdk: stop generating `build_property.ProjectDir` with a full path, and instead generate the `virtual_project_dir` config. (Again probably opt-in under some msbuild property.)

**Related:**
- Does CoreCompileInputs.cache contain more full paths? See also these previous efforts to make that path-independent:
  - https://github.com/dotnet/msbuild/pull/14559
  - https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/55514
- Do we need to solve full paths inside project.assets.json and other potential files similarly?
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Ensure analyzer config files are location-independent" (#86593)

Issues.Title: MSBuildWorkspace does not trim the entries of `TargetFrameworks`
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: 

- Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild 5.12.0 (5.12.0-1.26502.2+1324e1d3)
- .NET SDK 11.0.100
- Unchanged on `main` (da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24)

**Steps to Reproduce**:

`Lib/Lib.csproj` (note the space after the semicolon):

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFrameworks>net8.0; net10.0</TargetFrameworks>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

`Lib/C.cs`:

```csharp
public class C { }
```

Host (`net10.0`, references `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Workspaces` and `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild` 5.12.0):

```csharp
using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.MSBuild;

using var workspace = MSBuildWorkspace.Create();
workspace.RegisterWorkspaceFailedHandler(e => Console.WriteLine($"{e.Diagnostic.Kind}: {e.Diagnostic.Message}"));
await workspace.OpenProjectAsync(args[0]);
foreach (var project in workspace.CurrentSolution.Projects)
    Console.WriteLine($"'{project.Name}': {project.MetadataReferences.Count} metadata references");
```

Run `dotnet restore Lib/Lib.csproj`, then the host with the path of `Lib.csproj`.

**Diagnostic Id**: ---

**Expected Behavior**:

Both target frameworks load like in a command line build (`dotnet build Lib/Lib.csproj` succeeds for both, because MSBuild trims the entries of `TargetFrameworks`), each with its framework references (163 for `net8.0`, 167 for `net10.0` here), and the project names carry no whitespace.

**Actual Behavior**:

The second target framework is evaluated as `" net10.0"` (leading space), MSBuild rejects it, and the project loads without any metadata references. Every semantic query on it is wrong (all types are error types):

```
Failure: Msbuild failed when processing the file '...\Lib\Lib.csproj' with message: The TargetFramework value ' net10.0' was not
recognized. It may be misspelled. If not, then the TargetFrameworkIdentifier and/or TargetFrameworkVersion properties must be
specified explicitly.
'Lib(net8.0)': 163 metadata references
'Lib( net10.0)': 0 metadata references
```

(Message translated from a German MSBuild; the project name keeps the space.)

Other layouts that build fine on the command line fail the same way:

- A line break between the entries (`net8.0;` and `net10.0` on separate lines): the second project is named `Lib(` + line break + indentation + `net10.0)` and has 0 metadata references.
- A trailing semicolon (`net8.0;net10.0;`): an additional project `Lib` without target framework appears (1 metadata reference), and the load reports `Project does not contain 'Compile' target.`

**Cause**:

[`ProjectBuildManager`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24/src/Workspaces/MSBuild/BuildHost/Build/ProjectBuildManager.cs#L298) splits the property with `targetFrameworksValue.Split(';')` and sets each part as the global property `TargetFramework` without trimming it or dropping empty entries. MSBuild's own outer build turns `TargetFrameworks` into items (`_TargetFrameworks`), which trims whitespace and ignores empty entries, so `net8.0; net10.0`, a line break between the entries or a trailing `;` all work there.

**Suggested Fix**:

Split like MSBuild does, e.g. `targetFrameworksValue.Split(';', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries | StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries)` (or the equivalent for the `netstandard2.0` build of the build host), and use the trimmed value both for the global property and the project name.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "MSBuildWorkspace does not trim the entries of `TargetFrameworks`" (#86592)

Issues.Title: NullReferenceException when binding a cref in the documentation comment of a nested enum declared without body (`enum E;`)
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Workspaces 5.12.0 (`5.12.0-1.26502.2+1324e1d3`, latest on nuget.org), .NET SDK 11.0.100. The code paths below are unchanged on `main` (da9878a16).

**Steps to Reproduce**:

```csharp
class A { }

class O
{
    /// <summary>Refers to <see cref="A"/>.</summary>
    public enum E;
}
```

1. Parse with `DocumentationMode.Parse` or `Diagnose` (any language version from C# 12; the declaration itself produces no diagnostic).
2. Call `SemanticModel.GetSymbolInfo()` on the `NameMemberCrefSyntax`, or `SymbolFinder.FindReferencesAsync()` for `A`.

**Diagnostic Id**: CS1569 (symptom only: with `DocumentationMode.Diagnose` the crash surfaces as this error without location; the bug itself is in the binder, not in an analyzer)

**Expected Behavior**: The cref binds to `A`; Find References reports it.

**Actual Behavior**: `NullReferenceException`:

```
at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Binder.LookupMembersInternal(LookupResult result, NamespaceOrTypeSymbol nsOrType, ...)
at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.InContainerBinder.LookupSymbolsInSingleBinder(...)
at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Binder.LookupSymbolsInternal(...)
at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Binder.LookupSymbolsOrMembersInternal(...)
at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Binder.ComputeSortedCrefMembers(NamespaceOrTypeSymbol containerOpt, String memberName, ...)
at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Binder.ComputeSortedCrefMembers(CSharpSyntaxNode syntax, ...)
at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Binder.BindNameMemberCref(NameMemberCrefSyntax syntax, ...)
```

With `DocumentationMode.Diagnose`, `Compilation.GetDiagnostics()` reports the crash as CS1569 (error without location) for the project; a build that writes no documentation file is not affected.

Observations:
- `public enum E { }` binds fine, and so does the same body-less enum at namespace level.
- A nested `public class C;` binds fine.
- Every cref in that comment fails, whatever it refers to.

**Cause:** The `getBinder()` helper of [`MakeCrefBinder()`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24/src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/Binder/BinderFactory.BinderFactoryVisitor.cs#L1414-L1422) special-cases body-less declarations only for `TypeDeclarationSyntax`. `EnumDeclarationSyntax` is not one, so it reaches `factory.GetBinder(baseTypeDeclaration, baseTypeDeclaration.OpenBraceToken.SpanStart)` with the absent open brace, that is, position 0. [`VisitEnumDeclaration()`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24/src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/Binder/BinderFactory.BinderFactoryVisitor.cs#L685-L710) then treats position 0 as "in body": `IsBetweenTokens()` accepts every position when both brace tokens are `None` ([`IsBeforeToken()`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24/src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/Syntax/LookupPosition.cs#L93-L96)). It builds the outer binder at position 0, which is outside `O`, so `ContainingMemberOrLambda` is the global namespace, and `GetSourceTypeMember("E", ...)` returns `null`. The
`InContainerBinder` gets a `null` container, and the lookup throws. At namespace level the global namespace happens to contain `E`, which is why only nested enums are affected. `VisitTypeDeclarationCore()` already guards against default brace tokens ([L727](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24/src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/Binder/BinderFactory.BinderFactoryVisitor.cs#L727)); `VisitEnumDeclaration()` does not.

**Possible fix:** Handle body-less `EnumDeclarationSyntax` in `getBinder()` like body-less type declarations, and/or apply the default-token guard of `VisitTypeDeclarationCore()` to `VisitEnumDeclaration()`.

Issues.Title: Union case types not checked for accessibility consistency
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: 
- .NET version: 11.0.100
- Compiler version: '5.12.0-1.26452.1 (e42c0e42e89e41522593d0816707e71781ecbee2)'
- Language version: 15.0.

If there is a union type with a private inner type:
```csharp
public union Outer(string, Outer.Inner)
{
    private class Inner;
}
```
It compiles with no diagnostic. The lowered code contains a public constructor whose parameter type is the private nested class:
```csharp
[CompilerGenerated]
public Outer([Nullable(1)] Inner value)
{
	<Value>k__BackingField = value;
}
``` 


Switching over an instance of it using a `switch` expression outside the declared type where `Inner` is inaccessible:
```csharp
static string Describe(Outer outer) => outer switch
{
    string s    => "string",
};
```
reports:
> CS8509: The switch expression does not handle all possible values of its input type (it is not exhaustive). For example, the pattern 'Outer.Inner' is not covered.

However, adding it is not possible:
```csharp
static string Describe(Outer outer) => outer switch
{
    string s    => "string",
    Outer.Inner i => "inner"
};
```
as this reports:
> CS0122: 'Outer.Inner' is inaccessible due to its protection level

and

> CS8121: An expression of type 'Outer' cannot be handled by a pattern of type 'Outer.Inner'
The same happens with an `internal` case type switched over from another assembly.

[.NET Lab](https://lab.razor.fyi/#nVLNahRBECZiQPskPsFHLrsL6_5BQFcUohBQEEVvnuztKbMtneqxumaSEPbdPIsHX0HwDXwB6Z5xsyHowTo01VR9X1V9VebXvjFvJJ6IPZ24dP_nvjGmblbBOyS16h1csCnhLdUSzaUBgOkUz989PJw9WqK2qiSMwetGSSYvmEkG8AkcFS62JFQVzHXOpOL5BEfDAkPM7whPnnYe0plXty64rmK2HpNy2kH3ORiX6OaxueprNl8sljf78Wydo5T8KhCqhqARXhNqiUpOfWQEainsDDhfzJc4YtB5LRkZGfEj9KKmnn4AZzkPuiKsLVeBKqwuYLeqXE_vu5l01H9X5dl_qVLshjTZdorDlxSf_SvxNtuVN5ynLIBhxzPehY_6A6jFt1apP40SKizTKY6jwMXT2opPkcfQNYE-N761gViLTA_OxKsSw0VOKo3TKHlFQp_IKVXLP9109K8sNzb8q_KOkl3ysBu2taGhES6x2R7H7HBuNublLZfe373z9fuPb1_W925_2Dvf-w0)

**Expected Behavior**:
As per the [docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/proposals/csharp-15.0/unions), a union declaration is lowered to a struct declaration witha public constructor for each of the _case_types_. 

For a constructor written in source, a parameter type less accessible than the constructor triggers a [CS0051](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/compiler-messages/cs0051):
> Inconsistent accessibility: parameter type 'type' is less accessible than method 'method'.

I'd expect this declaration to be reported the same way.
If it's intended that case types can be less accessible than the union, I'd expect that to be documented, along with how consumers should write an exhaustive switch.



**Actual Behavior**:
- The declaration compiles with no errors, and the generated public constructor has a less accessible parameter type.
- A consumer's switch reports CS8509 naming the inaccessible type: "the pattern 'Outer.Inner' is not covered". Adding a case for it reports CS0122, so the warning can't be fixed by handling the case. (For comparison, a `closed` class `C` with a descendant that isn't visible at the switch site gives the same CS8509 but names the visible base type ("the pattern 'C' is not covered") and this behavior is [documented](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/proposals/csharp-15.0/closed-hierarchies#exhaustiveness-when-a-subtype-cant-be-used).)
- The only way to silence CS8509 is a _ or `var` arm, which swallows all other cases.

Issues.Title: Incremental parsing reports CS1513 at a stale position after reusing a node
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**:
- `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp` 5.12.0
- .NET SDK 10.0.404
- .NET runtime 10.0.15

Also reproduced with Roslyn commit `da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24`.

**Steps to Reproduce**:

1. Create a console project:

   ```xml
   <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
     <PropertyGroup>
       <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
       <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
     </PropertyGroup>
     <ItemGroup>
       <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp" Version="5.12.0" />
     </ItemGroup>
   </Project>
   ```

2. Add `Program.cs`:

   ```csharp
   using System.Linq;
   using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp;
   using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Syntax;
   using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Text;

   var oldTree = CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText("class C{/ // note\nx");
   var changedText = oldTree.GetText().WithChanges(new TextChange(new TextSpan(8, 0), "\n"));
   var incremental = oldTree.WithChangedText(changedText);
   var fresh = CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText(changedText);

   var oldX = oldTree.GetRoot().DescendantNodes().OfType<IdentifierNameSyntax>().Single();
   var newX = incremental.GetRoot().DescendantNodes().OfType<IdentifierNameSyntax>().Single();
   System.Console.WriteLine($"x reused: {oldX.IsIncrementallyIdenticalTo(newX)}");

   foreach (var (label, tree) in new[] { ("fresh", fresh), ("incremental", incremental) })
       System.Console.WriteLine($"{label}: CS1513 {tree.GetDiagnostics().Single(d => d.Id == "CS1513").Location.SourceSpan}");
   ```

3. Run `dotnet run`. The edit inserts a newline before the `/` token, making the final source `class C{\n/ // note\nx`.

**Diagnostic Id**: `CS1513`: `}` expected.

**Expected Behavior**:
Fresh and incremental parses of the same final text report `CS1513` at `[20..20)`, the position of the missing `}` token.

**Actual Behavior**:

```text
x reused: True
fresh: CS1513 [20..20)
incremental: CS1513 [11..11)
```

The incremental diagnostic location depends on edit history rather than the final text. Both syntax trees contain the same missing `CloseBraceToken` at `[20..20)`; only the diagnostic location differs.

The shift equals the width of the stale trailing trivia, ` // note\n`, so the diagnostic moves back nine characters, onto the previous line at the start of the `// note` comment. With different trivia the shift is a different size; with a bare `\n` it is one character.

**Impact**: The final text has syntax errors, so no invalid program compiles and no code generation changes. Editors that parse incrementally can show the missing-brace error at a different position, and on a different line, from a full build of the same file. Here the error appears on a comment.

**Root cause**:
`SyntaxParser.EatNode` consumes the reused `x` identifier without updating `_prevTokenTrailingTrivia`. Ordinary token consumption updates that field in `MoveToNextToken`. After the reuse, the field still holds the trailing trivia of the token consumed before `x`: ` // note\n` from the `/` token. The correct value is the trailing trivia of `x`, which is empty.

When the parser creates the missing `}`, `GetDiagnosticSpanForMissingNodeOrToken` checks the cached trivia for `EndOfLineTrivia`. If it finds one, it moves the diagnostic back by the trivia's full width. With the stale trivia this moves the diagnostic into earlier text. The reuse of `x` and the diagnostic shift are shown by the repro output; the private field transition is inferred from the source code.

**Proposed fix**:
After `EatNode` obtains `CurrentNode.Green`, set `_prevTokenTrailingTrivia` from that node's last terminal token, matching the state transition in `MoveToNextToken`:

```diff
             // remember result
             var result = CurrentNode.Green;
+            _prevTokenTrailingTrivia = result.GetLastTerminal().GetTrailingTriviaCore();
```

With this change it reports `CS1513` at `[20..20)` in both fresh and incremental parses.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Incremental parsing reports CS1513 at a stale position after reusing a node" (#86581)

Issues.Title: Don't offer IDE0370 for a suppression that makes a field-backed getter null-resilient
Issues.Body:
Fixes #86573

A `!` in the getter of a property that uses `field` can be what makes the getter null-resilient. Removing it makes the compiler report CS9264, but at the property or at a constructor's exit points, so the existing check, which only looks at diagnostics within the getter, didn't see it.

For these getters, the check now also looks at the type's diagnostics and at constructors declared in other partial declarations, and keeps the ones whose additional location is the property (CS9264 reports the property as an additional location). That covers the property name and the constructors, including an early `return` in a constructor, which is where the warning goes when not every path assigns the property, without letting unrelated warnings in constructor bodies block the fix.

Issues.Title: Incremental parsing drops lexical diagnostics from an interpolated string that becomes skipped text
Issues.Body:
# Incremental parsing drops lexical diagnostics from an interpolated string that becomes skipped text

**Version Used**:
- `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp` 5.12.0
- .NET SDK 10.0.404
- .NET runtime 10.0.15.

Also reproduced with Roslyn commit `da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24`.

**Steps to Reproduce**:

1. Create a console project:

   ```xml
   <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
     <PropertyGroup>
       <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
       <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
     </PropertyGroup>
     <ItemGroup>
       <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp" Version="5.12.0" />
     </ItemGroup>
   </Project>
   ```

2. Add `Program.cs`:

   ```csharp
   using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis;
   using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp;
   using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Text;

   var oldTree = CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText("class C { string M() => $\"{1 }}\"; }");
   var changedText = oldTree.GetText().WithChanges(new TextChange(new TextSpan(21, 2), ";"));
   var incremental = oldTree.WithChangedText(changedText);
   var fresh = CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText(changedText);

   foreach (var diagnostic in fresh.GetDiagnostics())
       System.Console.WriteLine($"fresh: {diagnostic.Id} {diagnostic.Location.SourceSpan}");

   foreach (var diagnostic in incremental.GetDiagnostics())
       System.Console.WriteLine($"incremental: {diagnostic.Id} {diagnostic.Location.SourceSpan}");
   ```

3. Run `dotnet run`. The edit replaces `=>` with `;`, producing `class C { string M() ; $"{1 }}"; }`.

**Diagnostic Id**: `CS8086`: A '}' character must be escaped (by doubling) in an interpolated string.

**Expected Behavior**:
Fresh and incremental parses of the same final text report the same diagnostics, including `CS8086` at `[29..30)`. The existing incremental parsing tests assert this through `CompareIncToFullParseErrors` in `IncrementalParsingTests.cs`.

**Actual Behavior**:

```text
fresh: CS8086 [29..30)
fresh: CS1519 [23..31)
incremental: CS1519 [23..31)
```

The incremental result depends on edit history rather than on the final text. The same loss affects other lexical diagnostics inside interpolated strings: six other edit sequences lose `CS8076`, `CS1039`, `CS8086`, and `CS1010`.

**Impact**: The final text already contains an error (`CS1519`), so no invalid program compiles and no code generation changes. The visible effect is a missing error in editors that parse incrementally, which can disagree with a full build of the same file until the next full parse.

**Root cause**:
The old interpolated-string expression contains `CS8086`, so the blender rejects that node. `Blender.Cursor.MoveToFirstChild` replaces the expression with a single `InterpolatedStringToken` built by `Lexer.RescanInterpolatedString`, which does not reconstruct lexical diagnostics. The diagnostic-free token passes the `CanReuse` diagnostics check and is reused as a token. The new parser then places it in `SkippedTokensTrivia`, so `ParseInterpolatedStringToken` never rescans it and the diagnostic a fresh lexer would attach is lost.

I found a TODO while investigating and I think it references this kind of issue. See `RescanInterpolatedString` in `Lexer_StringLiteral.cs`:

```csharp
// TODO: scan the contents (perhaps using ScanInterpolatedStringLiteralContents) to reconstruct any lexical
// errors such as // inside an expression hole
```

**Proposed fix**:
Make `Blender.Reader.CanReuse` reject `InterpolatedStringToken` so the edited text is lexed again. Interpolated-string expression nodes that are unaffected by an edit can still be reused as nodes.

An alternative is to resolve the TODO by having `RescanInterpolatedString` rescan the contents and attach the reconstructed diagnostics. That would keep token reuse but requires more lexer work. The proposed change is a smaller fix.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Incremental parsing drops lexical diagnostics from an interpolated string that becomes skipped text" (#86577)

Reject constructor reuse when parsing at global scope so the edited text is reparsed in its new context. In the issue reproduction, fresh and incremental parses now produce the same global statement, and both GetDiagnostics() and Emit() succeed.

Issues.Title: Incremental Script parse throws `InvalidCastException` in `GetDiagnostics` and `Emit` for valid source
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: 
- .NET SDK 10.0.404
- .NET Runtime 10.0.15
- Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp 5.12.0

I also checked against Roslyn commit da9878a16b492563fdcefc4259f2692fc07ddb24 and verified it is still the case.

**Steps to Reproduce**:

1. Create a csproj file with the content
```
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp" Version="5.9.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

2. Add Program.cs with the content:
```csharp
using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis;
using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp;
using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Text;

var oldTree = CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText(
    "void w() {} class C{w();",
    CSharpParseOptions.Default.WithKind(SourceCodeKind.Script));

var changedTree = oldTree.WithChangedText(
    oldTree.GetText().WithChanges(new TextChange(new TextSpan(20, 0), "}")));

CSharpCompilation.CreateScriptCompilation("repro", changedTree).GetDiagnostics();
```
3. Run it: `dotnet run`

**Expected Behavior**:
It would return a list (with CS0518 and CS1729), since the code is valid: `void w() {} class C{}w();`

**Actual Behavior**:
It throws an `InvalidCastException`. It occurs in `NamedTypeSymbol.GetScriptConstructor`

**Proposed fix**
In `LanguageParser.CanReuseMemberDeclaration`, handle `ConstructorDeclaration` separately and return `!isGlobal`. This prevents a constructor parsed inside the old class body from being reused at Script root after the edit, where the text should be parsed as a global statement. I tested it in a local build with this fix, and `GetDiagnostics()` and `Emit()` succeed.

Issues.Title: AffectedTests: any test-assembly change invalidates the map; support per-test invalidation and incremental map updates
Issues.Body:
### Environment
- .NET SDK 11.0.100, Microsoft.Testing.Platform, xUnit v3
- Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.AffectedTests 18.14.0-preview
- Local development with several git worktrees of the same repository, plus CI

### What happens
In our measurements, 59 of 63 local runs of our largest test project fell back to running every test. Three causes:

1. **The map identity includes a hash of the whole test assembly.** Adding or editing any single test changes that hash, so the map no longer applies and the whole project runs. In day-to-day work almost every change touches a test, so the selection rarely applies.
2. **Test UIDs are not portable across checkouts.** With xUnit v3, a test UID is derived from the absolute path of the test DLL. A map collected in one worktree (or on a CI agent) shares no UIDs with another checkout. Pinning a `.uniqueid` file per test project works around it, but this is not documented as part of the affected-tests workflow.
3. **Refreshing the map is expensive.** `--collect-test-map` runs the whole project with coverage (about 7 min in CI, over 15 min locally), and that is the only way to get a valid map again after cause 1.

### Expected
- Invalidate per test, not per assembly: a new or changed test method should only add or refresh its own entries, while the other tests keep their mapping.
- One run that executes the new/changed tests plus the tests affected by the changed sources, and updates the map incrementally from that run.
- Stable test identity across checkouts out of the box, or documentation of the supported way to get it.

### Why it matters
Without this, the feature mostly helps when only product code changes and no test is touched, which is rare in practice. With per-test invalidation, our largest project would drop from about 6.5 min to about 2 min per run.

### Alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

Issues.Title: Fix CLI resource generator source-build analyzer mismatch
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Condition the CLI resource generator’s `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Analyzers` package reference on `DotNetBuildSourceOnly != true`, matching the existing pattern in `src/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers/src/Directory.Build.props`.

As [reported by JanProvaznik](https://github.com/dotnet/dotnet/pull/11131#issuecomment-7101926988), source builds resolve a locally built analyzer package whose compiler reference is `42.42.42.42`. The running source-built compiler rejects it with CS9057, blocking SDK codeflow. This generator was introduced in dotnet/sdk#56378.

Normal builds retain the analyzers and their private-assets setting. Source builds omit only this development-time analyzer reference; the generator and its Roslyn API references remain enabled. No CLI behavior or public contract changes.

## Validation

- Reproduced the reported failure by building `Microsoft.DotNet.Cli.Resources.Generator.csproj` with `DotNetBuildSourceOnly=true` against the packages published by the failing [VMR source-build](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1693347): without the fix, compilation fails with CS9057 because the analyzer references compiler version `42.42.42.42` while the running compiler is `5.14.0.0`.
- Rebuilt the same project with the fix and the same packages: build succeeded, and the analyzer package was absent from the resolved dependencies while `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Common` and `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp` remained.
- A normal, non-source-build of the project also succeeded.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Full VMR source-build was not run locally; integrated source-build CI is needed to confirm the reported failure is resolved.

Documentation/agent-guidance pass: no updates needed for this internal build-only correction.

Issues.Title: Resolve HTML fingerprint placeholders for non-JavaScript assets
Issues.Body:
Fixes #57329

`OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders` filtered the endpoints to `.js` and `.mjs` before building both the import map and the label-to-URL map that resolves `#[.{fingerprint}]` placeholders. A stylesheet or an image that a project hard-fingerprints with `StaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern` was therefore renamed on disk at publish, while `index.html` kept linking the plain name and got a 404.

- Placeholders are now resolved against the endpoints of every asset; the import map and the preload links still only use JavaScript modules.
- Since the task now converts every endpoint, the assets are indexed by identity once instead of being scanned for each endpoint.
- Soft-fingerprinted assets, which include package `_content` assets, keep their plain path in publish as before. In build, where soft fingerprints are used too, a placeholder on a stylesheet now resolves to its fingerprinted endpoint, as it already did for scripts.

Tests:
- New unit tests in `OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholdersTest` for a hard-fingerprinted stylesheet and image, a soft-fingerprinted stylesheet in publish and in build, and an import map that stays JavaScript-only. The first three fail without the fix.
- `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.StaticWebAssets.Tests` unit tests (`FullyQualifiedName!~IntegrationTest`): no failures related to this change; the classes that need the full redist layout could not run locally.
- Built the task from `release/10.0.4xx` with the same change and published the `blazorwasm` template with hard-fingerprinted CSS on SDK 10.0.401: `index.html` links `css/app.<fingerprint>.css` and `bootstrap.min.<fingerprint>.css`, which match the published files, and the dev server serves both.

Issues.Title: OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders ignores the fingerprint placeholder on non-JavaScript assets, so a hard-fingerprinted stylesheet 404s after publish
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

In a standalone Blazor WebAssembly app with `OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders`, the `#[.{fingerprint}]` placeholder in `index.html` is only resolved for `.js` and `.mjs` assets. When a project opts a stylesheet or an image into hard fingerprinting with `StaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern`, publish renames the file on disk but `index.html` keeps linking the plain name, so the browser gets a 404.

### Steps to reproduce

1. `dotnet new blazorwasm -n BlazorCss` (the template already sets `OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders` and has the empty import map).
2. Add to `BlazorCss.csproj`:
   ```xml
   <ItemGroup>
     <StaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern Include="AppCss" Pattern="*.css" Expression="#[.{fingerprint}]!" />
   </ItemGroup>
   ```
3. In `wwwroot/index.html`, add the placeholder to the two stylesheet links:
   ```html
   <link rel="stylesheet" href="lib/bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min#[.{fingerprint}].css" />
   <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/app#[.{fingerprint}].css" />
   ```
4. `dotnet publish -c Release -o pub`

### Expected behavior

`pub/wwwroot/index.html` links the files that publish wrote:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="lib/bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.46ein0sx1k.css" />
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/app.nk9bgqz024.css" />
```

### Actual behavior

The placeholder is removed, but no fingerprint is added:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="lib/bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css" />
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/app.css" />
```

Only `css/app.nk9bgqz024.css` and `lib/bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.46ein0sx1k.css` exist in `pub/wwwroot`, so both stylesheets return 404 and the app renders unstyled. The same happens with other non-JavaScript assets, for example `favicon#[.{fingerprint}].png` with a `*.png` pattern.

### Is this a regression?

No. Placeholder overriding is new in .NET 10.

### Are there any workarounds?

Not with fingerprinting. Non-JavaScript assets have to stay soft-fingerprinted, which keeps their plain file names in publish, and get a hand-made cache-busting query string instead.

### dotnet --info output

```
.NET SDK:
 Version:           10.0.401
 Commit:            e34a38d2ae
 MSBuild version:   18.9.11+e34a38d2a

Runtime Environment:
 OS Name:     Windows
 OS Version:  10.0.26200
 RID:         win-x64
```

### Other details

`OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders.Execute` filters the endpoints to `.js` and `.mjs` before it builds the label-to-URL map that the placeholder replacement reads ([source](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/0a544cdef4893f75b9a44d0567258b890e79b15c/src/StaticWebAssetsSdk/Tasks/OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders.cs#L48)). A placeholder on any other asset therefore falls back to the plain path. The filter is right for the import map, which should only list JavaScript modules, but the placeholder replacement does not need it.

dotnet/aspnetcore#62211 declined fingerprinting CSS files automatically, because the SDK does not rewrite references between files and must not rename files the app links on its own. This issue is narrower: these files were already renamed on disk because the project asked for it, so only the `index.html` reference is missing and nothing has to be rewritten.

I have a fix that resolves placeholders against every asset type while the import map and the preload links stay JavaScript-only, and will open a PR for it.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders ignores the fingerprint placeholder on non-JavaScript assets, so a hard-fingerprinted stylesheet 404s after publish" (#57329)

Issues.Title: Stop re-analyzing recursive lambda and local-function calls in interprocedural dataflow analysis
Issues.Body:
Fixes #57327.

`PerformInterproceduralAnalysis` now bails out when the invoked lambda or local function is already being analyzed, that is, when its symbol is the owning symbol of the current analysis context or of any context in `MethodsBeingAnalyzed`. It handles that call the same way it already handles one past the maximum call-chain length: it resets the analysis data and returns the default value.

The existing guard compares whole analysis contexts. A recursive call always carries a different state, so that guard never catches recursion. Each recursive call site was therefore analyzed again down to `max_interprocedural_lambda_or_local_function_call_chain`, at every fixed-point iteration of every enclosing loop.

Scope:

- The new check applies only to lambdas and local functions. These are always analyzed context-sensitively and cannot be opted out through `interprocedural_analysis_kind`.
- Ordinary methods keep their current behaviour.

Precision trade-off: a recursive call is now treated like a call past the depth limit, after one level instead of three. Values that flow back out of a recursive invocation become unknown one level earlier. The non-recursive path through the function is still analyzed context-sensitively.

Effect on the repro from #57327 (time spent in CA1508): the small variant went from 3,883 s to 0.66 s with the same single diagnostic. The full variant went from not finishing in 15 CPU-minutes to 4.2 s, or 7.7 s together with #56414.

Tests:

- Added `RecursiveLocalFunctionsInvokedFromNestedLoops_CompletesAsync` (CA1508 null analysis). With the fix it passes in about 5 minutes, test discovery on a loaded machine included. Without the fix it was still running after 30 minutes.
- Ran the full `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers.UnitTests` suite with the fix on `release/11.0.1xx`, not on `main`, because `main`'s SDK 12 alpha could not be installed on my machine: 17,529 tests, 17,503 passed, 25 skipped, 1 failed. The failure was a nuget.org download error inside the test harness, and that test passed when re-run on its own.
- Not run: the full suite on `release/11.0.1xx` + #56414 + this fix, which is the closest match to `main`.

Issues.Title: Support version ranges in tool config.json files
Issues.Body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Today, tool config.json files can specify a version of a tool that everyone in a repo should use. However, tools often release updates, which causes churn to these files. If users could supply version range expressions for these ranges, then `tool install` and `tool update` commands could consume those ranges to seamlessly keep users up to date without having to change their source artifacts.  This would impact reproducibility, but be more usable.

### Describe the solution you'd like

I'd like config.json files to support range expressions.

With these range expressions
* `dotnet tool run` would not change at all - running of an already-installed tool should not pay any additional costs here
* `dnx` and the matching tool one-shot command would apply the range at download-check time in order to figure out which version to download and run
* `tool install` would apply the range at install-time to determine the maximal-safe tool version to install
* `tool update` would apply the range when determining which version to update _to_, if no specific version was given by the user as part of the command.
  * `dotnet tool update dotnet-ef` with config.json version of `[10, 11)` would update to the latest `10.x` version
  * `dotnet tool update dotnet-ef@11.*` would write the new range to the config.json (`[11, 12)`) and apply the range as above


### Alternatives you've considered

Instead of inferring some change to the config file as part of `update <tool>@<version>`, there could be a dedicated CLI flag to signal this intent. If that flag were passed, then any of the version-handling commands could reasonably cause updates to the config.json file.

### Additional context

_No response_
